rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari and most commentators understand the hypocrites’ “satans” as persistent evildoers who have become like satans.
rows.anchor: people "who, through their insolent persistence in evildoing (tamarrud), have become like satans" (Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad derives shaytan from remoteness from good and truth, and says the Qur’anic term can describe a person’s own evil impulses, especially those opposed to truth and morality.
rows.anchor: derived from the verb shatana, "he was [or 'became'] remote [from all that is good and true]"

rows.speaker: Raghib
rows.claim: Raghib explains the term’s Qur’anic use for satanic propensities in the soul, especially impulses contrary to truth and morality.
rows.anchor: all impulses which run counter to truth and morality (Raghib)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bond with God is the moral duty to use one’s innate intellectual and physical gifts as God intended.
rows.anchor: man's moral obligation to use his inborn gifts - intellectual as well as physical - in the way intended

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reason establishes this bond by revealing human weakness and dependence on a causal power, leading gradually to awareness of God’s will for conduct.
rows.anchor: faculty of reason which, if properly used, must lead man to a realization of his own weakness and dependence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the passage names no particular covenant, Asad reads the bond as an innate human relationship with God, recognizable by instinct and experience.
rows.anchor: there is no mention of any specific "covenant" in either the preceding or the subsequent verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links this innate relationship to God’s nearness to humanity and directs readers to his explanation of what God commands people to join.
rows.anchor: namely, that innate relationship with God which makes Him "closer to man than his neck-vein" (50:16)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address concerns the religious traditions the Israelites follow; here am means “rather” or “nay, but,” not an interrogative, because it is syntactically unconnected to the preceding sentence.
rows.anchor: sometimes - and especially when it is syntactically unconnected with the preceding sentence, as in this case

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this construction am is equivalent to bal and carries no question.
rows.anchor: it is an equivalent of bal ("rather", or "nay, but"), and has no interrogative connotation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In classical Arabic and ancient Hebrew, “father” could mean a grandfather, distant ancestor, or paternal uncle, explaining Ishmael’s inclusion as Jacob’s uncle.
rows.anchor: the term ab ("father") was applied not only to the direct male parent but also to grandfathers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmael is named before Isaac because he was Abraham’s firstborn son.
rows.anchor: Since he was the first-born of Abraham's sons, his name precedes that of Isaac

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The credit rule covers loans and commercial transactions, and tadayantum grammatically includes both the giver and receiver of credit.
rows.anchor: any transaction on the basis of credit, be it an outright loan or a commercial deal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scribe is to write in accordance with the laws laid down in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: in accordance with the laws promulgated in the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction literally says not to diminish any part of the undertaking, whose wording is entrusted to the debtor as the weaker party.
rows.anchor: the formulation of the undertaking is left to the weaker party, i.e., to the one who contracts the debt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A debtor may be unable to dictate because of physical disability, difficulty understanding business terms, or unfamiliarity with the contract language; weakness of understanding or body includes minors and mentally diminished elders.
rows.anchor: does not fully understand the business terminology used in such contracts, or is not acquainted with the language

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two-women provision does not question women’s moral or intellectual ability; Asad, citing ‘Abduh, attributes it to women’s usual lack of experience with business procedures and greater risk of mistakes.
rows.anchor: it is obviously due to the fact that, as a rule, women are less familiar with business procedures than men

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Writing down the contract means recording all rights and obligations that arise from it.
rows.anchor: all rights and obligations arising from the contract

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A scribe or witness must not be harmed by being held responsible for the contract’s consequences or either party’s failure to perform.
rows.anchor: held responsible for the eventual consequences of the contract as such, or for the non-fulfilment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on concealing testimony covers transaction witnesses and a debtor who accepted a trust-based loan without writing or witnesses and later denies the debt.
rows.anchor: a debtor who has been given a loan on trust - without a written agreement and without witnesses

rows.speaker: Ibn ‘Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas interprets the carried burdens as the sinners’ burdens of sin; Asad adopts this interpretation through Razi.
rows.anchor: interpretation given by Ibn 'Abbas, as quoted by Razi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means “unless my Sustainer wills a thing.”
rows.anchor: unless my Sustainer wills a thing

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: All commentators consider the bracketed command to do good to parents implied: it appears among prohibitions, although the Qur’an repeatedly enjoins filial goodness.
rows.anchor: In the consensus of all the commentators, the phrase interpolated by me between brackets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition on killing children may refer to abortions motivated by economic concerns.
rows.anchor: This may possibly refer to abortions dictated by economic considerations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The injunction warns against using brute force to pursue private interests.
rows.anchor: not resort to brute force whenever your private interests are involved

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Killing in pursuit of justice includes legal punishment, defensive war, and legitimate individual self-defence.
rows.anchor: the execution of a legal punishment or to killing in a just - that is, defensive-war

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once an orphan in one’s care comes of age, the guardian may use the property by borrowing or otherwise with the owner’s consent.
rows.anchor: the former guardian may "touch" his property, legally, by borrowing from it or otherwise utilizing it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal “in a manner that is best” implies that any use must aim to improve the orphan’s property.
rows.anchor: which implies the intent of bettering it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Full measure and weight represent equitable conduct in all dealings, not only commerce.
rows.anchor: refers metonymically to all dealings between men and not only to commercial transactions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God expects people to make their best effort toward equity, not achieve mathematical exactness, which is rarely possible in human dealings.
rows.anchor: God does not expect man to behave with "mathematical" equity

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads “when you speak” broadly as expressing an opinion on any subject, whether personally involved or not.
rows.anchor: According to Razi, the phrase "when you voice an opinion" (lit., "when you speak") applies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad thinks the mention of near kin makes the instruction especially likely to concern giving evidence in a dispute.
rows.anchor: the subsequent reference to one's "near of kin" makes it probable that the above injunction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to his explanation of the bond with God in 2:27.
rows.anchor: See surah 2, note 19

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means literally “to become scattered.”
rows.anchor: to become scattered

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic verb forms indicate Pharaoh threatened to cut off and crucify the sorcerers in great numbers, meaning either the converts were numerous or had many followers.
rows.anchor: either the repentant sorcerers thus addressed were many or, alternatively, that they had a large following

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possibility of a large following is supported by the Biblical report that many Egyptians joined Israel’s exodus.
rows.anchor: many Egyptians joined the Israelites in their exodus from Egypt: "And a mixed multitude went up also with them"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad’s rendering of min khilaf as “because of perverseness” is explained in his note on 5:33.
rows.anchor: As regards my rendering of min khilaf as "because of [your] perverseness", see surah 5, note 44

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking protection literally means seeking to become someone’s neighbour, invoking an ancient Arabian duty to protect and honour neighbours that Islam strongly affirms.
rows.anchor: a metaphorical expression denoting a demand for protection, based on the ancient Arabian custom

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi glosses “his place of security” as the seeker’s homeland.
rows.anchor: "his place of security" (ma'manahu)- i.e., "let him rejoin his homeland" (Razi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sending the protected person home leaves him free to accept or refuse the Qur’anic message and reaffirms that faith cannot be coerced.
rows.anchor: he is free to accept or not to accept the message of the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rizq means both physical and spiritual sustenance, accounting for references to heaven and earth as well as hearing and sight.
rows.anchor: used here in both the physical and spiritual connotations of this word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The addressed polytheists believe God exists but also assign divine or semi-divine qualities to beings they worship as intermediaries to approach Him.
rows.anchor: there are beings endowed with certain divine or semi-divine qualities, thus having, as it were, a "share" in God's divinity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This belief violates God’s oneness and uniqueness, depriving their belief in God of its true meaning and spiritual value.
rows.anchor: it deprives those people's belief in God of its true meaning and spiritual value

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the audience admits God creates and governs all and is ultimate reality, no other being can share in His divinity, however slightly.
rows.anchor: He is the One who creates and governs all things and is the Ultimate Reality behind all that exists

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal question means “How, then, are you turned away?” from the truth.
rows.anchor: "How, then, are you turned away?"-i.e., from the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What people invent includes false divine powers and deceptive half-truths such as luck, wealth, personal power, nationalism, and materialism, which obscure spiritual values and waste their lives.
rows.anchor: deceptive ideas and "glittering half-truths meant to delude the mind" (see 6:112 and the corresponding note)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob disbelieved the wolf story and inferred from his sons’ envy that they had harmed Joseph, yet his hope in 12:83 shows he was not certain Joseph had died.
rows.anchor: knowing his sons' envy of Joseph, at once realized that it was they themselves who had done grievous harm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s words literally mean that he turns to God for aid against the misfortune his sons described.
rows.anchor: it is to God that I turn for aid against what you are describing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God grants a person’s desires when divine wisdom deems their satisfaction ultimately beneficial; min qualifies the request as receiving something from what was asked.
rows.anchor: provided that His unfathomable wisdom regards its satisfaction as ultimately beneficial to the human being concerned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baqiyat as-salihat means good deeds whose fruit endures forever, and the expression also occurs at 19:76.
rows.anchor: ("good deeds, the fruit whereof endures forever") occurs in the Qur'an twice - in the above verse as well as in 19:76

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally compares these deeds as better in God’s sight for merit and for hope.
rows.anchor: "are better in thy Sustainer's sight - as regards merit, and better as regards hope"

rows.speaker: Al-Qadi ‘Iyad
rows.claim: Al-Qadi ‘Iyad, quoted by Razi, says sinners’ good deeds count on Judgment Day but are outweighed by their godlessness.
rows.anchor: whatever good such sinners may do is far outweighed by their godlessness (Al-Qadi 'Iyad, as quoted by Razi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the sequence also appears in 27:7 and 28:29, Asad thinks Moses was lost in the desert; this may symbolize his dawning need for spiritual guidance.
rows.anchor: Moses had lost his way in the desert: probably a symbolic allusion to his dawning awareness that he was in need of spiritual guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This episode belongs to Moses’ wanderings after his flight from Egypt, as described from 28:14 onward.
rows.anchor: the period of his wanderings subsequent to his flight from Egypt (see 28:14 ff.)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad treats the fire as an allegory of the Bible’s burning bush and refers to his note on 27:7-8.
rows.anchor: the allegory of the "fire" - the "burning bush" of the Bible - see note 7 on 27:7-8

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: According to the Itqan, this Meccan surah belongs to the final group of Meccan revelations; its title reflects its repeated references to earlier prophets.
rows.anchor: which according to the 'Itqan belongs to the last group of the Meccan revelations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah’s main theme is God’s oneness, uniqueness, and transcendence as the core of prophetic revelation, a truth people often forget or ignore.
rows.anchor: the core of all prophetic revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophets’ stories show the continuity and unity of revelation and religious experience; belief in one God entails one community and brotherhood among true believers across outward labels.
rows.anchor: this community of yours is one single community, since I am the Sustainer of you all

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The truth being cast against falsehood is God’s transcendence, which rejects the idea that God is immanent in or coexists with creation.
rows.anchor: the truth of God's transcendence against the false idea of His existential immanence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The finite, perishable universe cannot be a projection of its Creator, who is infinite and eternal.
rows.anchor: The obvious fact that everything in the created universe is finite and perishable effectively refutes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about what people attribute to God also means defining Him; treating God as immanent in creation attempts to define His Being.
rows.anchor: the idea of God's "immanence" in His creation is equivalent to an attempt to define His Being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who do not commit fully to their professed faith may assign decisive influence over destiny to real or imagined forces, thereby granting them divine qualities.
rows.anchor: attribute to all manner of extraneous forces, be they real or imaginary, a decisive "influence" on his own destiny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal wording is “this, this is the far-away straying”; Asad refers to his explanation of this paraphrase at 14:18.
rows.anchor: "this, this (dhalika huwa) is the straying far-away"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title comes from a word in 26:224; although some commentators place the last four verses in Medina, Asad says available evidence places the whole surah in mid-Meccan period, six or seven years before the Hijrah.
rows.anchor: all the available evidence shows that the entire surah belongs to the middle Mecca period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects Suyuti’s Medina dating of 26:197 based only on its mention of Israelite scholars, since such references also occur in Meccan revelations.
rows.anchor: as Suyuti does, that verse 197 belongs to the Medina period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah stresses human weakness and self-deception, which lead most people to reject revelation and obvious moral values and worship power, wealth, glory, slogans, or fashionable ideas.
rows.anchor: the unchanging character of man's weakness and proneness to self-deception

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to his note on 7:85 and says Shu‘ayb’s story with Midian is told in greater detail at 11:84-95.
rows.anchor: is given in greater detail in 11:84-95

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad dates the surah to late Meccan period before surah 17, while some authorities place verse 85 at Juhfah during the Prophet’s flight to Medina.
rows.anchor: verse 85 was revealed at a place called Juhfah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title was apparently taken at random from al-qasas in verse 25, perhaps because about half the surah recounts Moses’ story.
rows.anchor: The conventional "title" appears to have been taken at random from the word al-qasas occurring

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account emphasizes Moses’ human impulses, perplexities, and errors to counter pious tendencies to give prophets superhuman or semi-divine qualities.
rows.anchor: depicts the purely human aspects of his life - that is to say, the impulses, perplexities and errors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah ends by affirming that only God is divine and all things perish except His eternal Self.
rows.anchor: sonorous evocation of the truth that "there is no deity save God", and that "everything is bound to perish, save His [eternal] Self"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the explanation of Moses’ desert wandering and of the fire allegory, Asad refers readers to his notes on 20:10 and 27:7-8.
rows.anchor: For an explanation of Moses' wanderings in the desert, see note 7 on 20:10

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders al-tur as Mount Sinai throughout because he understands the Qur’anic term to refer invariably to that mountain.
rows.anchor: the noun at-tur ("the mountain") is being rendered as "Mount Sinai"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted phrase means that Moses sought news about which route the family should take.
rows.anchor: as to which way we are to pursue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most authorities call the surah one of the last Meccan revelations, while some classify it among the earliest Medinan revelations.
rows.anchor: Most of the authorities are of the opinion that this surah is one of the last to have been revealed in Mecca

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other scholars divide the surah, assigning its opening ten or eleven verses to Medina and its main body to Mecca, or the first nine to Mecca and the rest to Medina.
rows.anchor: scholars who hold the opposite view, ascribing the first nine verses to Mecca

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad concludes that historically the surah marks the transition between the Meccan and Medinan periods.
rows.anchor: On the whole, it would seem that, historically, the surah marks the transition between the Mecca and Medina periods

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title comes from the spider-house parable, which symbolizes false beliefs and values eventually swept away by truth.
rows.anchor: a symbol of false beliefs and false values, which in the long run are bound to be blown away by the winds of truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah was revealed in the middle Meccan period and takes its title from Luqman’s counsel to his son in verses 12-19.
rows.anchor: Luqman owes its title

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad sees no sound basis for commentators’ claim that some verses belong to the Medinan period.
rows.anchor: There is no cogent reason to ascribe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The diminutive “my little son” is an idiomatic term of affection regardless of whether the son is young or grown.
rows.anchor: a diminutive idiomatically expressive of endearment irrespective of whether the son is a child or a grown man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fisāl literally describes weaning that takes place within two years.
rows.anchor: weaning is [or "takes place"] within two years

rows.speaker: philologists
rows.claim: Some philologists use fisāl for the whole period of conception, gestation, birth, and earliest infancy, when a child is wholly dependent on its mother.
rows.anchor: According to some philologists, the term fisal circumscribes the entire period of conception, gestation, birth and earliest infancy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gratitude to parents accompanies gratitude to God because parents enable one’s birth while God is the ultimate cause and source of existence.
rows.anchor: gratitude towards parents, who were instrumental in one's coming to life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: References to the Battle of the Confederates, especially verse 20, indicate that this passage was revealed immediately after the year-5 AH battle.
rows.anchor: the tone of these references, and especially of verse 20, shows that this part of the surah was revealed immediately after that war

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage on the Prophet’s marriage to Zaynab was revealed in year 5 AH, probably a few months before the Confederates passage; verses 4-5 indirectly allude to Zayd’s adoptive relationship.
rows.anchor: Verses 37-40, which deal with the Prophet's marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 28-29 and 52 date no earlier than year 7 AH and may be later; the remaining chronology is uncertain, though Suyuti places much of the surah after surah 3 and before surah 4.
rows.anchor: verses 28-29 and 52 cannot have been revealed earlier than the year 7 H., and may even belong to a later period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah’s complex form reflects its revelation in stages across the Medinan period and its varied material about the Prophet, his family and contemporaries, and rules particular to his wives.
rows.anchor: revealed in small segments at various times between the end of the first and the middle of the last third of the Medina period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although classical commentators give many explanations of amanah, Asad finds the most convincing readings to be reason or intellect and the faculty of volition, the ability to choose good or evil.
rows.anchor: the most convincing of them (mentioned in Lane 1, 102, with reference to the above verse) are "reason", or "intellect", and "the faculty of volition"

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari explains that humanity took up reason and relative free will but failed to meet the moral responsibility they entail; this describes the human race, not necessarily every individual.
rows.anchor: failed to measure up to the moral responsibility arising from the reason and the comparative free will with which he has been endowed" (Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad supplies “God speaks” because the possessive in “servants of Mine” refers to God.
rows.anchor: the possessive pronoun in the subsequent phrase "servants of Mine" obviously relates to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s earth being wide means people can always do good and spiritually migrate from evil toward God; Asad links this enduring sense of hijrah to 4:97.
rows.anchor: there is always a possibility of doing good and "migrating from evil unto God" - which is the permanent, spiritual connotation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revealed immediately after the preceding surah, this one continues the theme of reasoned acceptance or wilful rejection of revelation.
rows.anchor: this one continues the theme begun in the latter; man's reasoned acceptance or wilful rejection of divine revelations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title comes from fussilat in verse 3, describing the Qur’an’s messages as clearly spelled out.
rows.anchor: The title is derived from the verb fussilat occurring in verse 3

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to repel evil with what is better refers here to scurrilous objections and hostile criticism of the Qur’an; the passage continues the argument of verse 26 and parallels 13:22 note 44.
rows.anchor: the injunction to "repel [evil] with something that is better" relates to scurrilous objections to, and hostile criticism of, the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah’s title comes from the participle adh-dhariyat in verse 1; Suyuti dates its revelation to about two years before the Prophet’s emigration to Medina.
rows.anchor: according to Suyuti, about two years before the Prophet's exodus to Medina
